title: Batter Pant, Pant banter: India's two-sided show stealer in Wellington
excerpt: When on song with the bat, Rishabh Pant doesn't spare anyone. Neither does he with his words, not even his own teammates
author: Bharat Sundaresan
body: “Main leg spin daal sakta hoon….ganda sa action chahiye toh Jaiswal daal sakta hai…”

It was one of the many standout lines that emanated from behind the stumps, courtesy Rishabh Pant as New Zealand battled away late on Sunday. It was Pant imploring his captain Shubman Gill to throw him the ball for some “leg spin” as the visitors looked to find a way to break the partnership between Devon Conway and Rachin Ravindra. His other suggestion was Yashasvi Jaiswal with the “ugly action”.

It was during a period of play when the forever-ebullient wicket-keeper had found his voice. Not like he generally goes too long without finding it. But this was Pant at his absolutely menacing best with his keeping gloves on. And nobody was going to be spared. Starting with his bowlers but including the other fielders and the opposition batters. Even if most of his banter was in Hindi. Even if most of it made little sense at times to anyone else but Pant.

“He is ready to mingle..” he yelled out at one point towards the end of the over as Conway shouldered his arms to a delivery outside off-stump. The New Zealand opener didn’t seem to fathom what Pant was on about, neither did any of his Indian teammates around the bat.

It wasn’t all just random though. There were things that the 29-year-old was noticing about the surface and how the Kiwi batters were dealing with it too. Not surprisingly, since his eyes do catch everything.

“Yeh length mein dikkat ho raha hai,” he exclaimed at one point while Henry Nicholls was still out batting, having started from where he left off in the first innings. It was after an Anshul Kamboj delivery that pitched around 9 meters from the pitch, just short of a good length, and cramped the left-hander, who jammed his bat down uncomfortably at the ball. “He’s having some issues with this length,” is what Pant was trying to tell his captain.

As it turned out, this happened to be a rather prudent observation. For, Gill immediately pivoted to a new plan, one where he crammed the leg-side up with fielders, leaving only a ring field of three on the off-side. In came the leg gully, a square leg, a deepish short leg, a short mid-wicket and a couple of others to this side, as Kamboj and Prasidh Krishna, who’d just entered the attack, began peppering that length repeatedly from around the wicket.

It took only a handful of overs before Krishna had Nicholls prodding at one, getting an inside-edge and having him caught brilliantly by Dhruv Jurel who dived forward and clung on to a spectacular short-leg catch. The plan had worked. The trap had been successful, and India had got rid of probably their biggest thorn en route to a famous win at the Basin Reserve.

The Nicholls’ wicket is what triggered Pant’s most vocal session, which lasted for the rest of the day’s play. At one point, he even screamed, “Chup nahi hona abhi..” (We can’t go quiet here) when Ravindra and Conway started to get their eye in. To their credit, the two Wellingtonian left-handers survived the remaining hour or so and will resume on Day 5 as the home team look to salvage a famous draw on a pitch which still continues to remain largely in their favour. Despite all of Pant’s efforts to keep his teammates entertained and the Kiwi batters on their toes.

It had been the Rishabh Pant show all day long though. He’d been at his menacing best with bat in hand during the first half of the day scoring his 9th Test hundred, and probably among his most destructive yet. The stage had been set for the enigmatic wicket-keeper well before he even strode out to bat the previous evening. And he didn’t disappoint. It started off as a calculated assault but soon turned into a brutal and merciless onslaught as Pant tore into a tired Kiwi attack with some shots even wildly outrageous by his own standards. There were also the usual array of ramps and reverse ramps, even a reverse paddle, and a range of big hits while he moved and rolled around his crease.

If the Black Caps weren’t already batted into the ground by the likes of Jaiswal, Rahul, Gill and Devdutt Padikkal, Pant simply got them to tap out and submit. And like always, it was as entertaining as ever. No wonder so many of his peers talk about the Rishabh Pant way being the most envious of methods to play cricket. His innings included six sixes, taking him within 30 of Ben Stokes’ all-time record—138 in 122 Tests. Pant has 108 and this is still only his 53rd Test. His runs tally is ticking along rather rapidly too, with the Indian dynamo now 9th on the all-time list for wicket-keepers with most Test runs. But within 600 runs of jumping into the top 5. The form he’s in, it shouldn’t take too long for him you’d think.

For now, though, Pant’s focus like with the Indian team, will be on getting his bowlers ready to mingle with a pitch that has played hard to get so far in terms of providing any joy to them, and in turn creating a lot more dikkat for the Kiwi batters as they look to hang on grimly. Regardless, Rishabh will be there chatting away and holding court as always.
